text: Okay, before we take our first intervenor because of the confusion about public utility property taxes, I am submitting a memo as a commission exhibit number one. And Ryan, do you want to pass this out, please, to all of the parties? Oh, and give one to the court reporter, please. And I'm going to read into the record the relevant information. It occurred to me that the testimony that we have had so far was all over the board about what taxes utility property pays. And I I just want to clear the record. So statewide assessment in West Virginia public utility property is assessed by the the state under West Virginia code chapter 11-6. The board of public works determines the assessed value of public utility property. The state tax commissioner as chief executive of the state tax division administers the preparation of tenative assessments for consideration and final determination by the board of public works including reviewing company information returns and preparing valuation recommendations. The state auditor allocates the assessment values among the counties and calculates the county taxes assess or based on the assessment rates in each county. The valuation is based on a combination of property net book cost and a calculated value of property based on net operating income. And I've got some examples, but I'm not going to read that into the record. It'll speak for itself. After the board of public works determines the total assessed value, the state auditor aortions the assessed value among the counties in which the utility operates. The allocation can be based on direct assignment of taxable income to a county or an allocation formula. The taxable value of large high-cost facilities that may be located in a single county but which serve the entire utility system are not allocated to only the county containing the facility. The state auditor determines the taxes for each county using applicable levy rates of each county applied to the assessed valuation allocated to each county. Within a limited time period, a utility may appeal a valuation or petition for relief from an erroneous assessment pursuant to West Virginia code. A company operating large electric transmission facilities in West Virginia but having no other utility operations in the state are evaluated the same as public utilities that have production transmission and distribution operate operations in West Virginia. The lack of local generation or distribution operations or lack of local revenue and income does not mean that the transmission facilities must be valued solely by netbook cost. Under the unit method, if applicable, the state may consider the value of the integrated transmission business as a whole and determine a portion of net operating income attributable to West Virginia and then apply the capitalization rate to that net operating income. And with that, I'm going to move that be in the record. And hopefully that will clear up the record as to how utility property is assessed and taxed in West Virginia. Now, let's go to our first intervenor. What?

text: So, the the issues of cost allocation and reliability violation are I don't want to say inseparable but very closely tied together in this instance because what we're talking about are large load customers and to oversimplify a data center is a machine that turns electricity into money. just that that is their primary input is electricity and to some extent chips and such. To the extent that a data center company a company looking to site or build a data center believes that it can get cheap electricity, subsidized transmission buildout, things like that in the vicinity that affects their siting choices. Those are the inputs that they use in their business when they decide where they want to go. And if those conditions change, as we've seen and as is laid out in my testimony in a couple PJM utilities that I specifically note, uh those data centers will uproots and leave. I mean it it in many cases they do not have significant investments in terms of site control anything like that. They basically come to the local utility and said hey we would like to build this massive facility. Um can you you know what would be involved? and they've done that maybe six or seven or eight times at different places in the same utility or to different utilities in the same zone or in different zones. the end effect of one of those zones or a FERC essentially making it an all of PJM thing that no you know let's because again the the FERC show cause order I don't want to misummarize it or pretend that I know what FERC is going to decide but the the [clears throat] thrust of the FERC order seems to imply that there is something unjust about the way that PJM currently allocates transmission costs for large load customers. So it follows logically that whatever FERC decides might increase the share that large load customers pay for their own interconnections. That is the sort of economic input that makes a data center go you know what I I think I'd like to go further west maybe you know there's this new development in in whatever state. So that's the reason that these two issues are like this because to the extent that cost allocation favors data centers that increases the data center load that we see in sort of this self-fulfilling cycle and if that cycle breaks then we may see significant drops in whether projected data center load or the rate at which projected data center load actually materializes depending on how responsive LSEs are to those changing market conditions and whether the data center companies that no longer intend to build data centers bother to call the LSEs and let them know those plans have been cancelled.
